30-006.r: Normal annual rainfall, decreasing → Kochi, Kolkata, Patna, Delhi (exam answer); 2024 data: Kochi 2828.09 mm, Kolkata 2089.6, Delhi 732.714, Patna 619.031.

30-007.r: Mango shower → pre-monsoon (April) showers in Karnataka and Kerala, from Bay of Bengal thunderstorms; they help mangoes ripen early and stop premature dropping.
30-007.c: A mango shower is pre-monsoon rain, not a crop, so (d) does not fit; (c), the only rain option, fits better, though mango showers belong to Kerala and Karnataka, not Bihar and Bengal.

30-008.r: Mango shower → coastal Karnataka (and Kerala); Blossom shower → Kerala; Norwesters → West Bengal; Loo → Punjab to Bihar.

30-010.r: Mango showers → pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and coastal Karnataka at the end of summer; help early ripening of mangoes ('April rains').

30-011.r: Mango Shower → pre-monsoon showers in Kerala, coastal Karnataka and Tamil Nadu that help early ripening of mangoes.

30-012.r: Norwesters (Kal-Baisakhi) → storms of West Bengal, Assam and Northeast; first moisture for Assam's tea and Bengal–Assam rice; Karaburan → hot dusty wind of central Asia.

30-013.r: Least rainfall → Leh (56.967 mm, 2024); Jaisalmer 451.888 mm, Bikaner 457.611 mm, Cherrapunji 10207 mm.

30-015.r: Cherrapunji (now Sohra) → East Khasi Hills district, Meghalaya; record rainfall place after Mawsynram.

30-016.r: Highest rainfall (over 250 cm a year) → Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayan region and Meghalaya.

30-017.r: India is a 'thirsty land' despite 1257 mm rain → all reasons: rain packed into June–September, rapid runoff and quick evaporation; dry for the other eight months.

30-018.r: Rainwater harvesting → cost-effective water strategy (embankments, tanks; raises the water level); Tamil Nadu is the leading state.

30-019.r: About 200 mm (20 cm) average annual rain → north of the Zaskar range in J&K (now Ladakh) and western Rajasthan; answer (b) Jammu and Kashmir.

30-020.r: Jharkhand → gets its rain from the South West Monsoon (June to September).

30-021.r: Map question: shaded part of India → mean annual rainfall 100 to 150 cm (answer a).
30-021.c: The book marks (a) 100–150 cm, but its explanation says the shaded area gets 100 to 200 cm.

30-022.r: Very heavy rain in the Pushkar Hills → floods in the Balotra region (Rajasthan).

30-023.r: IMD 'rainy day' → a day with rainfall of 2.5 mm or more in 24 hours.

30-024.r: A and R true, R explains A: monsoon rain in the Ganga plain falls toward the west and north-west (Punjab about 600 mm, Gangetic plain up to 1500 mm).

30-025.r: Map question → it shows the All India water divide.

30-026.r: Chennai warmer than Kolkata → latitude; Himalayan snowfall → altitude; rain falling from West Bengal to Punjab → distance from sea; Sutlej-Ganga plain winter rain → western depressions.

30-027.r: Watershed development in semi-arid India → hallmark is a system of tanks storing water from seasonal rivers (about 120,000 small tanks).

30-028.r: Desert Development Programme (started 1977-78) → 131 blocks of 21 districts in 5 states up to 1994-95; now 235 blocks of 40 districts in 7 states.

30-029.r: A and R true, R explains A: inland waterways are poorly developed because most of India gets rain only four months a year, so rivers lack water.

30-030.r: Cherrapunji (now Sohra) → on the Khasi Hills, Meghalaya.
30-030.t: Not the Garo, Naga or Mikir Hills.

30-031.r: Lowest South-West monsoon rain (1 June–30 September) among options → Chennai; Chennai gets most rain from the North-East monsoon.

31-001.r: Winter rain in India's northern plains → Western Disturbance: extratropical storms from the Mediterranean bringing sudden winter rain to the north-west.

31-002.r: Winter rainfall → Punjab (Western Disturbance) and coastal Tamil Nadu (65–75 cm from the retreating North-East monsoon).

31-003.r: A and R true, R explains A: Tamil Nadu coast is dry in SW monsoon (parallel to Bay branch; rain shadow of Arabian branch); winter rain from NE monsoon.

31-006.r: A and R true, R explains A: most of India is dry in winter as north-east trade winds blow land to sea, carrying little moisture (except Tamil Nadu coast).

31-008.r: North-East monsoon rain → Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu coast, southern Andhra), also south-east Karnataka and south-east Kerala.

31-010.r: A true, R false: winter anticyclones form with high pressure and low temperature; North India's winter rain comes from western disturbances and does not cause them.

31-011.r: Winter rain → North-West (western disturbance: Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, west UP) and South-East (Tamil Nadu coast, North-East monsoon, October–December).

31-012.r: Western Disturbance winter rain in the north-western plain → decreases from west to east; non-monsoon rain from Mediterranean storms driven by the westerlies.

31-013.r: Rabi (winter) crops → mainly Punjab and Haryana (Indo-Gangetic Plains); their winter rain comes from extra-tropical cyclones steered by the westerlies, not tropical ones.
31-013.c: Two readings: R wrongly calls the winter-rain storms tropical cyclones (they are extra-tropical western disturbances), which strictly gives (b); ignoring that slip, (a). The book accepts both.

31-014.r: North-west India's winter rain → western disturbances (a weak form of cyclonic disturbance, so they are the best answer over 'cyclonic depression').

32-001.r: 2004 Tsunami (26 December, Indian Ocean) → worst hit the Coromandel Coast (south-east coast, False Divi Point to Kanyakumari).

32-002.r: Hudhud cyclone → hit the Andhra Pradesh coast at Visakhapatnam, October 2014; name suggested by Oman.

32-003.r: Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) → at INCOIS, Hyderabad; working since October 2007.

32-004.r: India Meteorological Department (1875, Ministry of Earth Sciences) → head office at Lodhi Road, New Delhi; first head office Kolkata; IITM is in Pune.

32-005.r: Floods → plains of UP and Bihar; earthquakes → Himalayan foothill zone; droughts → mid-eastern India; cyclones → Jharkhand and northern Odisha.

32-006.r: A and R true, R explains A: Himalayan landslides have increased due to large-scale mining (roads, dams, minerals) and more earthquakes.

32-007.r: More cyclones in the Bay of Bengal → high temperatures create low pressure; cyclones spin anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere, clockwise in the southern.

32-008.r: A and R true, R not the reason: east coast is more cyclone-prone because Bay of Bengal cyclones strike it; it also lies in the north-east trade wind zone.

32-009.r: A and R true, R explains A: Koyna dam (Maharashtra) sits on an old fault plane that reservoir water-level changes may activate → more earthquakes.

32-010.r: Odisha → faces the most natural disasters (cyclones, floods, droughts) due to its Bay of Bengal coast.

32-011.r: First Disaster Management Training Institute (by CRPF) → Latur, Maharashtra; India's first such institute was set up at Nagpur on 29 April 1957.

32-012.r: India has 4 seismic zones (2, 3, 4, 5) on the BIS map; Karnataka Plateau is not high-intensity, unlike Uttarakhand, Kutch, Himachal Pradesh.

32-014.r: Seismic zones → Bhuj V, Srinagar V, Hyderabad II, Chennai III; so Bhuj–IV, Hyderabad–I and Chennai–II are all wrong.
32-014.c: The book gives no single answer (*): three of the four pairs are wrong.

32-015.r: A and R true, R explains A: floods in North Indian plains have risen as silt deposition made river valleys shallower.

32-016.r: Most flood-prone state of India → Bihar.

32-017.r: Uttar Pradesh → eastern areas are most flood-affected; the high-flood zone is 48% of UP's flood-affected area.

32-018.r: True: disasters hurt developing countries most; Bhopal gas tragedy (December 1984, MIC leak) was man-made; mangroves reduce cyclone impact. False: India is disaster-free.

32-019.r: Flood → plains of UP and Bihar; Earthquake → Himalayan zone; Drought → West and Central India; Tsunami → southern coastal India.

32-020.r: Cyclone Tauktae → formed in the Arabian Sea; hit the Gujarat coast in May 2021.

32-021.r: Tropical cyclone in May → local temperature variation (book's answer); needs warm moist air, strong Coriolis force, unstable troposphere, no strong vertical wind shear.

32-022.r: Ockhi → extremely severe cyclonic storm that hit India's coast in November 2017.

32-023.r: Tauktae → hit India's western coast in 2021 (Arabian Sea, 14–19 May; Gujarat, Maharashtra); Amphan (May 2020) hit West Bengal, Odisha, Bangladesh.

32-024.r: Fengal → cyclone of late November–early December 2024 from the southwestern Bay of Bengal; crossed northern Tamil Nadu and Puducherry coasts.

33-001.r: Regur (black) soil → formed by weathering of basaltic lava; also called black cotton soil, tropical black earth or tropical chernozem.

33-002.r: Black cotton soil → from weathering of fissure volcanic (basaltic) lava of the Deccan trap; covers plateaus of Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, MP, Chhattisgarh; ideal for cotton.

33-003.r: Regur → black soil (from Telugu 'Reguda'); most widespread in Maharashtra, also MP, Karnataka, AP, Gujarat, Telangana; covers 5.46 lakh sq km.

33-005.r: Black cotton soil → Regur; a mature soil with high water retention; 'self-ploughing' as it develops wide cracks when dry.

33-006.r: A true, R false: Deccan Trap Regur is black but poor in humus, nitrogen and phosphorus; rich in alumina, iron, lime, magnesium carbonates, potash; best for cotton.

33-008.r: Karewas (thick glacial clay with moraines, Kashmir Himalaya) → famous for Zafran (saffron) cultivation.

33-009.r: A true, R false: black soil suits cotton because it is clayey, holds moisture long and 'self-ploughs' (cracks when dry), not because of humus.

33-013.r: Lava soil → black soil of western India (Deccan trap); the predominant soil of the Malwa Plateau.

33-015.r: Black soil → needs little irrigation: high moisture retention; 'self-ploughed' as loose particles fall into its cracks.

33-016.r: Black soil in Jharkhand → Rajmahal hill region (NIDM report).

33-017.r: Wrong: black soil is found in the Himalayan region. Regur is mainly in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka, MP; a mature, moisture-retentive soil good for cotton.

34-001.r: Laterite → red (iron and aluminium oxides), poor in nitrogen, lime, humus; tapioca and cashew grow well; found in South Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala, Meghalaya, not Rajasthan/UP.

34-002.r: Only 1 true: laterite forms under high temperature and heavy rainfall; it is low in humus, nitrogen and phosphorus, so statement 2 is false.

34-003.r: Only 1 true: laterite (Latin 'Later' = brick) forms with high temperature and rainfall; leaching removes lime and silica, leaving it rich in iron oxide and aluminium.
34-003.h: Later = brick: laterite is brick-red and used like brick.

34-004.r: Not true: laterite is moisture-retentive with much clay. Laterite is porous, well-drained, acidic, leached, poor in lime and nitrogen, and a good building material.

34-005.r: A true, R false: net sown area is about 60% in West Bengal vs 40% in Andhra Pradesh; Andhra's soils are mainly red and alluvial, not laterite.

34-006.r: Laterite → Maharashtra (south), predominant in the Malabar coastal region; leached by alternate wet and dry seasons, poor in lime, rich in iron and aluminium oxides.
34-006.t: Laterite is NOT rich in lime.

34-009.r: Laterite soil → made infertile by excess iron (iron oxides).

35-001.r: Alluvial soil → rich in potash, phosphoric acid, alkalies; low in nitrogen; very fertile; covers about 45.6% (15 lakh sq km). Reh, Thur, Chopan are saline soils.
35-001.t: Reh, Thur, Chopan, Kallar are names of saline soils, not alluvial.

35-002.r: Alluvial soil → most fertile, productive soil of India; low in nitrogen; formed from Himalayan sediments and sea retreat; covers 15 lakh sq km.

35-003.r: Alluvial soil → deposited by rivers; Khadar = new alluvium on floodplains (fresh layer each flood); Bangar = old alluvium above flood reach.

35-004.r: All four true: alluvial soil's sand content falls west to east; it occurs as Bangar and Khadar; covers about 40% of India; rich in potash, poor in phosphorus.
35-004.t: Keys differ: this question accepts 'poor in phosphorus', while another in this chapter keys 'rich in phosphoric acid'.

35-005.r: Alluvial soil → largest, most widespread soil group of India (about 15 lakh sq km, 45.6%); widest in the Indo-Gangetic plain, Punjab to West Bengal and Assam.

35-007.r: Old alluvium (Kachhari clay) of the Gangetic plain → Bhangar: above flood level, with calcareous concretions; Khadar is the newer alluvium.
35-007.t: Bhangar = old alluvium; Khadar = new alluvium.

35-008.r: Minimum water retention → alluvial sand soil (sandy soils saturate sooner; clay loam holds more water).

35-009.r: Loamy soil → has all particle types: about 40% sand, 18% clay, 42% silt.

35-010.r: Lowest pH among Chhattisgarh soils → Bhatha (laterite), about 6.5, acidic and leached, found in higher areas.

36-001.r: Alluvial → Uttar Pradesh; Black → Maharashtra; Red → Andhra Pradesh; Desert → Rajasthan.

36-002.r: Western Rajasthan soils (Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Barmer, Jodhpur etc.) → alkaline, saline, with a calcareous base → high calcium content.

36-003.r: Pea (a legume) → enriches soil nitrogen by fixing atmospheric nitrogen; others: clover, soybeans, alfalfa, lupins, peanuts.

36-004.r: Black Gram (Urd) → grown to improve soil fertility; also used as fodder.

36-005.r: Red soil's colour → ferric oxides; formed from ancient crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks; poor in lime, phosphates, nitrogen, humus; fairly rich in potash.

36-006.r: A false, R true (book): red soil is the third largest group (about 10.6% of India's area); it surrounds black soil on the south, east and north.

36-007.r: Zinc → most deficient micronutrient in Indian soils.

36-008.r: A false, R true: Himalayan soils lack humus, though the Himalayas have the largest area under forest cover.

36-009.r: Karewa soil → Kashmir Valley (Kashmir Himalaya); used to grow Zafran, the local saffron.

36-010.r: Soil water available to plants → maximum in clay soil (highest water retention; slow air movement keeps water).

36-011.r: Particle diameter → clay below 0.002 mm; silt 0.002–0.05 mm; fine sand 0.05–2 mm.

36-012.r: Not true: (a) on Matasi's height relative to Bhata and Kanhar. Matasi (red-yellow) covers 55–60% of Chhattisgarh; iron-rich, sandy, less fertile than Kanhar; prime paddy soil.

37-001.r: Usar soil → pH above 7 (alkaline); treated with pyrites, gypsum, green manure (not lime); tolerant paddy varieties (Narendra Usar Paddy) can be grown.
37-001.t: Lime treats acidic soil; gypsum treats Usar (alkaline) soil.

37-002.r: Fertile soil for common crops → pH six to seven; pH below 7 is acidic, above 7 alkaline.

37-003.r: Lime → used to make acidic soil cultivable; very acidic or alkaline soil is unfit for common crops.

37-004.r: Soil salinity and alkalinity → long-term remedy is gypsum in the fields (with about one foot of water for leaching).

37-006.r: Largest alkali-affected area (exam key) → Uttar Pradesh (2129.61 sq km in a 2019 atlas); largest saline or salt-affected area → Gujarat.

37-009.r: Salinization (salts left as irrigation water evaporates) → makes some soils impermeable, hinders germination and growth, cuts yields; common in arid irrigated regions.

37-010.r: A and R true, R explains A: saline soils (excess sodium, potassium, high magnesium, little lime) are unfit for crops; salt builds up from dry climate and poor drainage.

37-011.r: Tea → best on slightly acidic soil without calcium; needs heavy rain but no stagnant water, so grown on hill slopes.

38-001.r: Critical soil erosion → Shivalik/Western Himalayan foothills, Chambal–Yamuna ravines (most affected: Chambal valley), Chotanagpur Plateau, Maharashtra black soil, arid Haryana–Rajasthan–Gujarat.

38-003.r: Morena (Chambal valley, MP) → soil erosion problem; gully erosion (Chambal ravines) has also made Bhind, Gwalior and Shivpuri barren.
